Meru: the mountain at the centre of the earth in the Puranas, and the head bead of a rosary; hence the chief, the best. The body as a chariot with a charioteer is the image of the Katha Upanishad; here the chariot is the bent of people's nature in each age, and the charioteer what leads it.
470.2: By the First Guru (Guru Nanak Dev Ji). The Sama (Veda) calls the Master Setambar (the white-robed), who dwells in truth; (in its age, people) abide in truth; everyone merges in the Truth. The Rig (Veda) says: (Ram) pervades all; among the gods, the Name of Ram is the sun; by taking the Name, sins depart; O Nanak, then (people) attain liberation. In the Yajur (Veda), Chandravali was beguiled by force, and (the Master's name) became Kaanh Krishna, the Yadav; he brought the Parjat (tree) for the gopi, and made merry in Brindaban. In Kalyug the Atharva Veda came (to the fore), and (the Master's) name became Khuda and Allah; taking blue cloth, they wore garments (of it), and the Turks and Pathans held sway. All four Vedas came to be (held) true; those who read and ponder them find four (different) teachings (in them). One who, worshipping with loving devotion, calls himself lowly, then, O Nanak, attains liberation. ॥2॥

The four Vedas are set beside the four ages: the Sama with Satjug, the Rig with Treta, the Yajur with Duapar, the Atharva with Kalyug, each with the name of the Lord that then prevailed: Setambar, Ram, Krishna, Allah. Chandravali: by tradition a gopi of Braj whom Krishna loved. The Parjat: the wish-fulfilling tree of Indra's heaven, which by the Puranas Krishna brought down to earth for his queen Satyabhama. Blue was the dress of the Turk and Pathan rulers of the time.
470.3: I am a sacrifice to the True Guru, meeting whom (I have) kept the Master in mind; who, giving his teaching, has given (me) the collyrium of wisdom, by which with these eyes (I) have seen the world (as it is). Those traders who left the Master and clung to another have drowned. The True Guru is the ship; rare is the one who has understood (this); (him the Guru) in his grace has carried across. ॥13॥
470.4: Salok, by the First Guru (Guru Nanak Dev Ji). The simmal tree is straight, very tall and very stout; (the birds) that come to it in hope: why do they go away disappointed? (Because) its fruits are insipid, its flowers tasteless, and its leaves of no use. O Nanak, sweetness and lowliness are the very core of virtues and good deeds. Everyone bows for his own sake; no one bows for another's. Put on the scales and weighed, the (pan) that sinks is the heavier. The sinner who slays deer bows double; (but) what comes of bowing the head, when (people) go on with impure hearts? ॥1॥
The simmal (silk-cotton) tree: tall, straight and bright with red flowers, but its fruit holds nothing to eat, only floss.
470.5: By the First Guru (Guru Nanak Dev Ji). (The pandit) reads the books, says the sandhya prayers, and disputes; he worships stone (idols), and sits in trance like a heron; lies are on his lips, (decked out) like fine ornaments; three times a day he ponders the three-footed (Gayatri); a rosary round his neck, a tilak on his brow; two dhotis, and a cloth over his head. If he knew the work of (worshipping) God, (he would see that) all these rites are surely hollow. Says Nanak, one should meditate (on God) with firm faith, (but) without the True Guru one does not find the way. ॥2॥

Sandhya: the Brahmin's prayers and rites at dawn, noon and dusk; the three-footed one (traipal) is the Gayatri, the Rig Veda verse in three parts recited at them. The heron stands still in the water as if in trance, but is watching for fish.
470.6: Leaving the lovely garment (of the body) and its beauty in the world, one has to go; the bad and the good one has done, one must oneself reap. (One who) gave orders as his mind pleased must go hereafter by a narrow road; stripped bare, he is driven to hell, and then he looks dreadful indeed. Having done wrong, he must repent. ॥14॥
471.1: Salok, by the First Guru (Guru Nanak Dev Ji). Compassion the cotton, contentment the thread, continence the knots and upright conduct the twist: such is the soul's sacred thread; O pandit, if you have it, put it on (me). It does not break, no dirt clings to it, it is not burned, nor is it lost. Blessed, O Nanak, are the people who go (on their way) wearing it round their necks. (This thread) you had brought for four cowries and, seated in the chauka, put it on (your patron); you whispered instruction in (his) ear, and the Brahmin became (his) guru. He died, it fell away, and he went without a thread. ॥1॥
Chaukar: four cowries; the cowrie shell was the smallest money.
471.2: By the First Guru (Guru Nanak Dev Ji). (One commits) countless thefts, countless adulteries, countless lies and countless abuses; countless frauds and breaches of trust, kept secret within, night and day. From cotton the thread is spun; the Brahmin comes and twists it; a goat is killed, cooked and eaten, and everyone says: (the thread) is on. When it grows old it is cast aside, and then another is put on. O Nanak, were there strength in the thread, the thread would not break. ॥2॥
471.3: By the First Guru (Guru Nanak Dev Ji). By believing in the Name, honour springs up; praise (of God) is the true thread; (with it, honour) is gained in the Lord's court; this pure thread will not break. ॥3॥
471.4: By the First Guru (Guru Nanak Dev Ji). There is no thread on the senses, no thread (to hold him back) from women; (so) morning after morning his beard is spat upon. No thread on the feet, no thread on the hands; no thread on the tongue, no thread on the eyes. Without a thread himself he wanders about, yet twisting threads, he puts them on others. He takes a fee and performs marriages, and, taking out his almanac, shows (people) the way. Hear and see, O people, this wonder: blind in mind, and his name is Wise. ॥4॥
471.5: When the Master grows merciful and shows grace, he will have (one) do that very work (which pleases him). That servant alone serves whom (the Master) makes obey his Hukam. By obeying the Hukam (he) is approved, and then he will reach the Master's mansion. Doing what pleases the Master, he will gain the fruit his mind longed for; then he will go to the Lord's court robed in honour. ॥15॥
471.6: Salok, by the First Guru (Guru Nanak Dev Ji). You levy a tax on the cow and the Brahmin; by the cow-dung (you plaster with) no one crosses over. Dhoti, tilak and rosary (you wear), (yet) you eat the grain of the mlechhas. Indoors you worship, (outside) you read the Kateb; your way of life, brother, is the Turks'. Give up these hypocrisies; taking the Naam, you will cross over. ॥1॥

By the commentaries, these lines speak to the Hindu officials of the Muslim rulers, who levied the rulers' tax even on cows and Brahmins and yet kept the rites of purity: the kitchen square plastered with cow-dung, the dhoti, tilak and rosary. Mlechh: impure, alien; the caste Hindus' word for foreigners, here the Muslim rulers.
471.7: By the First Guru (Guru Nanak Dev Ji). Those who devour men say the namaz; those who ply the knife have the sacred thread at their necks. In their homes the Brahmins blow the conch; they too relish the same flavours. False is the capital, false the trade; by speaking lies they get their food. Modesty and dharma dwell far away (from them); O Nanak, falsehood fills every place. A tilak on the forehead, an ochre dhoti round the waist, (and) a knife in the hand: (they are) butchers of the world. Wearing blue clothes, they find favour (with the rulers); taking their bread from the mlechhas, they worship the Puranas. Their food is a goat slaughtered with the words of a foreign tongue, (yet they say:) no one is to step onto our chauka. The chauka is laid out and a line drawn (around it); and the false ones come and sit upon it. (They say:) take care, lest it be defiled, lest it be defiled; this food of ours will be spoiled. With defiled bodies they do wicked deeds, and with soiled minds they rinse their mouths. Says Nanak, let the True One be meditated on; if there is purity, then the True One is found. ॥2॥

The devourers of men: by the commentaries, the officials of the time who preyed on the people by bribes and oppression; those with the knife and the sacred thread are their Hindu clerks. The foreign tongue (abhakhia): Arabic, in which the kalma is recited as the goat is slaughtered halal. Chuli: a handful of water sipped and rinsed in the mouth for ritual purity.
472.1: (God) holds everyone in his mind, and, watching (them), moves them along under his eye. He himself bestows greatness, and he himself has (beings) do their deeds. Greater than the great is he, and vast his earth; one by one he sets each to his task. If he turns his look against them, he makes sultans (worth no more than) grass; they beg at the door, and no one puts alms (in their bowl). ॥16॥
472.2: Salok, by the First Guru (Guru Nanak Dev Ji). If a thief robs a house, and, having robbed it, gives (the goods) for his forebears, then in the world beyond the goods are recognised, and (so) he makes thieves of his forebears. The hands of the go-between (the Brahmin) are cut off: such is the justice (God) does. O Nanak, in the world beyond one receives only what one earns, toils for and gives (with one's own hands). ॥1॥

Pitars: dead forebears. In the shraadh rite, food and goods are given to a Brahmin for them, in the belief that they reach the forebears; the Brahmin who takes them is the go-between (dalal) of this salok.
472.3: By the First Guru (Guru Nanak Dev Ji). As a woman's monthly course comes to her time after time, (so) in the mouth of the false dwells the defilement (of falsehood), and day after day he comes to grief. They are not called pure who (merely) wash the body and sit down (as pure); O Nanak, they alone are pure in whose mind he (God) has come to dwell. ॥2॥
472.4: (Those who have) saddled horses swift as the wind, and harems decked out in every colour, (who) have set up houses, pavilions and mansions and sit (in them), having spread out a display, (who) take the pleasures their minds desire, but do not know the Lord: they lose (the game of life). Giving orders, they ate (their fill), and gazing at their palaces forgot death; old age came upon them, undone by their youth. ॥17॥
472.5: Salok, by the First Guru (Guru Nanak Dev Ji). If Sutak is to be believed in, then Sutak is everywhere: in cow-dung and in wood, too, the worm comes to life; of all the grains of corn there are, not one is without life; first of all, water itself is a living thing, by which every being is kept green (alive). How then can Sutak be kept away? Sutak falls in the very kitchen. O Nanak, Sutak is not removed in this way; (divine) knowledge washes it off. ॥1॥
In a house under sutak, its food and water are not touched and no rites are performed.
472.6: By the First Guru (Guru Nanak Dev Ji). The Sutak of the mind is greed; the Sutak of the tongue is falsehood; the Sutak of the eyes is gazing on the beauty of another's wife and on another's wealth; the Sutak of the ears is that (people) backbite and it falls into the ears. O Nanak, (such) men, (though they look as white) as swans, go bound to the city of Jam. ॥2॥
472.7: By the First Guru (Guru Nanak Dev Ji). All Sutak is doubt (superstition); it clings to those who have gone after another (than God). Birth and death are (God's) Hukam; by his will (a being) comes and goes. Eating and drinking are pure: (God) has gathered sustenance and given it (to all). O Nanak, those who have understood (this) through the Guru are touched by no Sutak. ॥3॥
473.1: Let us praise the True Guru as great, in whom are great excellences. When the Husband Lord brought (us) together (with the Guru), then (those excellences) came into sight; when it pleased him, (he) set them to dwell in the mind. By his command, laying his hand on (our) forehead, he struck the evils out from within. With the Husband Lord pleased, the nine treasures were found. ॥18॥
473.2: Salok, by the First Guru (Guru Nanak Dev Ji). First (the Brahmin) makes himself pure, and comes and sits in the pure (chauka); before him, the pure one, is set (food) that no one has gone near to defile. Pure, he eats, and begins to chant a salok; (yet the food) is thrown into a foul place (the belly): on whom does this blame fall? Grain is a god, water is a god, fire is a god, salt (is a god); the fifth, ghee, was added, and then (the food) became clean and holy. (Then this) body (of the gods) met with the sinner, and was spat upon. The mouth with which (people) do not utter the Naam, and without the Name eat dainties: O Nanak, know it in the same way: on that mouth spittle falls. ॥1॥
473.3: By the First Guru (Guru Nanak Dev Ji). Of woman we are born, within woman we are formed, to woman we are betrothed and wed; through woman friendships are made, through woman the way (of the world) goes on; if a woman dies, (another) woman is sought; through woman the bonds (of kinship) are tied. Why should she be called bad, of whom kings are born? Of woman, woman herself is born; without woman there is no one. O Nanak, the True One alone stands outside woman (unborn of her). The mouth with which (God) is ever praised glows with the beauty of good fortune; O Nanak, those faces are radiant in that True Court. ॥2॥
Bhand is here an old word for woman, not the jester (bhand) of present-day speech.
473.4: Everyone claims (things) as his own; the one who does not is to be sought out and singled out. For what each has done, each must himself settle the account. Since we are not to stay in this world, why wear ourselves out in pride? Call no one bad: having read the letters, this is what is to be understood; do not quarrel with a fool. ॥19॥
473.5: Salok, by the First Guru (Guru Nanak Dev Ji). O Nanak, by speaking harshly, body and mind grow harsh. The harsh one is known as harsh, and harsh is the harsh one's repute; the harsh one is cast out of the Lord's court, and spittle falls on the harsh one's face; the harsh one is called a fool, and is punished with (a beating of) shoes. ॥1॥
473.6: By the First Guru (Guru Nanak Dev Ji). Those who are false within, keep up an honour outside and make a show in the world: though they bathe at the sixty-eight places of pilgrimage, their filth does not come off. Those with silk within and rags without are the good ones in the world; their love is set on God, and they dwell on the thought of seeing him. In (his) love they laugh, in love they weep, and they fall silent too; they care for no one but the True Master. On the road (of life) they ask at his door for provisions, and eat when he gives. There is one court and one pen, and there we and you (all) are to meet; at that door he takes the account, and, O Nanak, (the false) are crushed as seeds are crushed for oil. ॥2॥
474.1: You yourself made the creation, and you yourself have set your power (in it). Setting out the pieces, raw and ripe, you watch what you have made. Whoever has come will depart; each one (goes) when his turn has come. Why put out of mind the Master to whom our soul and breath belong? With our own hands, by ourselves, let us put our own task in order. ॥20॥
474.2: Salok, by the Second Guru (Guru Angad Dev Ji). What kind of love is this, that goes and attaches itself to another? O Nanak, he is called a lover who stays ever absorbed (in the Beloved). One who takes it as good when good comes, and turns sour when ill comes: such a one is not called a lover; he deals by keeping accounts. ॥1॥
474.3: By the Second Guru (Guru Angad Dev Ji). One who both bows in salute and answers back (to the Master) has gone astray from the very start. O Nanak, both are false; neither is accepted. ॥2॥
474.4: The Master by serving whom peace is found: let us keep him ever in mind. Since what we have done (comes back) to us, why labour at what is evil? Let us do no evil at all, and look far ahead. Let us cast the dice in such a way that we do not lose (the game) with the Master; let us labour at something that brings profit. ॥21॥
474.5: Salok, by the Second Guru (Guru Angad Dev Ji). (If) a servant is at his service, and with it is proud and quarrelsome, (and) talks a great deal, he does not win the Master's pleasure. If he gives up his self and serves, then he gains some honour; O Nanak, he meets the one he serves; (so) engaged, he is accepted. ॥1॥
474.6: By the Second Guru (Guru Angad Dev Ji). What is in the heart is what sprouts; what the mouth says is (mere) wind. One sows poison and asks for Amrit: see what justice this is. ॥2॥
474.7: By the Second Guru (Guru Angad Dev Ji). Friendship with the ignorant never turns out well; as he understands, so he behaves; let anyone weigh it and see. One thing goes into another only when what was there is set aside. With the Master no command prevails; it is prayer, offered (to him), that befits. Practising falsehood, falsehood alone comes of it; O Nanak, through (God's) praise (the mind) blossoms. ॥3॥
474.8: By the Second Guru (Guru Angad Dev Ji). Friendship with the ignorant, and love for one far greater (than oneself), are like a line drawn in water, which leaves neither place nor trace. ॥4॥
474.9: By the Second Guru (Guru Angad Dev Ji). If one who is ignorant takes up a task, he cannot bring it to a good end; even if he does one thing or so well, he spoils the next all the same. ॥5॥
474.10: A servant is (truly) at service if he walks as the Master wishes; he receives great honour, and draws double wages besides. (If) he sets himself up as the Master's equal, he then falls into disgrace; he loses the wages he had, and is struck with shoes on the face. He whose gifts we eat: to him let us give praise. O Nanak, with the Master no command prevails; prayer prevails. ॥22॥
474.11: Salok, by the Second Guru (Guru Angad Dev Ji). What kind of gift is it that one gets of oneself (by one's own effort)? O Nanak, that is grace (karamat) which comes when the Master is pleased. ॥1॥
Karamat is here a gift of grace, not a miracle: it answers the daat (gift) of the line before.
475.1: By the Second Guru (Guru Angad Dev Ji). What kind of service is this, that does not take away the fear of the Master? O Nanak, the one to be called a servant is he who merges into the Master. ॥2॥
475.2: O Nanak, no end is seen to the Lord's near and far shores. He himself brings about the making, and then he himself brings about the destroying. Round the necks of some are chains; many ride on horses. He himself causes and he himself does; to whom am I to complain? O Nanak, he who made the creation: it is he again who must care for it. ॥23॥
475.3: Salok, by the First Guru (Guru Nanak Dev Ji). (God) himself fashioned the vessels (of the body), and he himself fills them. Some hold milk, while others stay up on the hearth; some lie down and sleep on quilts, while others stay standing over them (in attendance). He sets right those, O Nanak, on whom he looks with grace. ॥1॥
475.4: By the Second Guru (Guru Angad Dev Ji). He himself fashions, he himself makes, and he himself keeps, too, what he has brought forth; creating beings within it, he watches them, setting up and pulling down. To whom can we speak, O Nanak? He himself is all in all. ॥2॥
475.5: Of the greatness of the Great One, nothing at all can be said. He is the Creator, the Master of creation, the Bountiful (Karim); he carries their sustenance to all beings. (All beings) do the work that he himself has allotted (to them) from the very start. O Nanak, apart from the One there is no other place; he does whatever is his will.
Sudh (corrected): written after the closing numbers of the vaar, it marks that the text was checked against the original.
475.6: There is one God, Ik Oankar, the One who pervades all and is ever the same; his Name is Sat (the One who truly is); he is the Creator, the Being who dwells in all, without fear, without enmity, his form beyond time, unborn, self-existent, realised by the Guru's grace. Raag Asa, the hymns of the Bhagats. Kabir Ji, Namdev Ji, Ravidas Ji. Raag Asa, the hymn of Sri Kabir Ji. Falling at the Guru's feet, I pray and ask: for what has the soul been placed (in the body)? For what purpose is the world born and destroyed? Tell me, and make me understand. O divine Guru, be kind: set me on the path by which the bonds of fear are broken, and the soul is freed at the root from the pains and pleasures of birth and death that its own deeds have brought. (The soul) does not tear apart the nooses and bonds of Maya, and (its) mind takes no shelter in Sunn; (it) has not recognised its own true state, free of desire; in this way (its) hardness is not ended. (The world) that nowhere arises (apart from God), (the mind) takes to have arisen, for it cannot tell what is from what is not. When the mind's thinking of rising and setting (birth and death) was destroyed, then it was absorbed for ever in Sahaj, its attention fixed (on God). As, when the pot of water breaks, the reflection merges into its original (the thing it mirrored), says Kabir: so has the delusion of the rope (taken for a snake) fled; then the mind is absorbed in Sunn. ॥4॥

Gun here is a rope: in the dark a rope looks like a snake, and so, through delusion, the world seems to be apart from God. The bimb is the original (the sun or moon) whose reflection falls in the water of the pot; when the pot breaks, the reflection is no longer separate.
476.1: Raag Asa, the hymn of Bhagat Kabir Ji. (Those who) wear dhotis three and a half yards long and put on sacred threads of triple strands, who have rosaries round their necks and gleaming lotas (water pots) in their hands, cannot be called Sants of the Lord: they are the thugs of Banaras. Such Sants do not please me, who swallow the tree along with its branches. (They) scour their pots before setting them (on the fire), and wash the firewood before they burn it; they dig up the earth to make two hearths, (yet) they eat up men whole. Those sinners go about ever doing wrong, and with their mouths call themselves Apras (those who touch no one). For ever and ever they go about in pride, and drown their whole families (too). To whatever (God) has set anyone, to that he is set, and he does deeds to match. Says Kabir: one whom the True Guru meets does not come into birth again. ॥4॥
476.2: Raag Asa, the hymn of Bhagat Kabir Ji. The Father has given me comfort; (my) bed is restful, and (he) has put Amrit in (my) mouth. Why should I let that Father slip from my mind? Going on (to the world beyond), I shall not lose the game (of life). My mother (Maya) is dead, and I am at ease indeed; I do not wear the padded coat (of the body), and the cold does not touch me. I am a sacrifice to that Father who has given me (a new) birth, (and) has ended my company with the five (passions). I have slain the five and put them under my feet; my mind and body are soaked in Simran of the Lord. My Father is the great Gosain; how shall I go to that Father? When the True Guru met (me), he showed (me) the way, (and) the Father of the world became dear to my mind. (O God,) I am your son, and you are my Father; the two of us have one dwelling place. Says Kabir: (your) servant has understood the One alone; by the Guru's grace I have come to see everything. ॥4॥
476.3: Raag Asa, the hymn of Bhagat Kabir Ji. (They) fill one vessel with cooked fowl, and fill another vessel with water (wine); all around sit the five yogis, and in their midst is the noseless queen. The drum of the noseless one (Maya) beats on, loud and resounding; (O Maya,) only some rare one of discernment has cut you down. The noseless one dwells within all; having struck all down, she keeps looking about (for more). (She says:) I am sister and niece to all; to the one who weds me, I am a maidservant. My husband is truly discerning; he alone is called a Sant. He stands firm over my head; no one else comes near me. (The Sants) have cut off her nose, cut off her ears, and hacking her to pieces, have cast her out. Says Kabir: she is the enemy of the Sants, and the darling of the three worlds. ॥4॥

The noseless one (nakti) is shameless Maya, who keeps faith with no one. In the Darpan's reading the five yogis are men given to the five passions, in whose minds Maya sits enthroned as queen; some commentators see here a rite of the left-hand tantrics.
476.4: Raag Asa, the hymn of Bhagat Kabir Ji. Yogis, celibates, ascetics, sannyasis, those who roam to many places of pilgrimage, those who have their hair plucked out, those girdled with munj grass, the silent ones, those with matted hair: even so, in the end they must die. So it is Ram who should be served. One who has Ram's Name on the tongue and love (for it within): what can Jam do to him? (Those who) know the Shastras, the Vedas, astrology and grammars by the score, (who) know all the tantras, mantras and medicines: even so, in the end they must die. (Those who enjoy) the pleasures of kingship, the royal canopy and the throne, many beautiful women, betel, camphor and fragrant sandalwood: even so, in the end they must die. I have searched the Vedas, the Puranas and the Simritis, all of them: nowhere (in them) is there escape. Says Kabir: so I repeat (the Name of) Ram, who wipes out birth and death. ॥4॥
477.1: Raag Asa, the hymn of Bhagat Kabir Ji. The elephant plays the rebab, the ox plays the pakhavaj, the crow beats the cymbals; putting on a dancer's robe the donkey dances, and the he-buffalo sings the songs of devotion. The Sovereign Ram has cooked fritters of frost; some rare one of understanding (alone) has eaten them. Sitting at home the lion prepares betel leaves, and the bandicoot brings the folded betel; in house after house the mice sing songs of joy, and the tortoise blows the conch. The son of the barren woman sets out to be wed, and canopies of gold are spread; (he) has wedded a maiden lovely in form, and the hare and the lion have sung (the couple's) praises. Says Kabir: listen, O Sants: the ant has eaten up the mountain; the tortoise says: I want a burning coal as well. (Thus) has this Shabad of hidden meaning been told. ॥4॥

This hymn speaks in inverted images: Ram has made the impossible happen, and only a rare one understands it. In the Darpan's reading the animals are the mind's old natures (the elephant pride, the ox sloth, the crow cunning, the donkey lust, the buffalo stubbornness), now turned to the Lord's praise; the barren woman's son is the mind born of Maya, setting out to wed an understanding untouched by vice.
477.2: Raag Asa, the hymn of Bhagat Kabir Ji. (One whose) pouch is the One (Name), whose bag is the body of seventy-two (channels), the bag that has a single door, (who) begs (for the Name) in the land of nine regions (the body itself): that yogi is the most excellent in the world. Such a yogi obtains the nine treasures; he takes the Brahm (the soul) that lies below (in Maya) and raises it to the Gagan. Making wisdom his patched coat and meditation the needle, he twists the thread of the Shabad and puts it through; making (the body of) the five elements his deerskin seat, he walks on the Guru's path. Making compassion his ash-scraper and the body his fire-pit, he kindles the fire of (true) vision; he keeps love for him within his heart, and stays absorbed in trance through all four ages. All yoga is the Name of Ram, whose are the body and the breath of life. Says Kabir: if (God) shows mercy, he grants the true mark. ॥4॥

The batua is the yogi's pouch for sacred ash, the adhari his shoulder bag, the mirgani his deerskin seat, and the fahuri the scraper that gathers the ash of his fire-pit. The body's single door is the Tenth Gate, and its nine regions are its nine openings.
477.3: Raag Asa, the hymn of Bhagat Kabir Ji. Where have the Hindu and the Turk (Muslim) come from? Who set these ways going? Think it over in your heart and reflect, you wrangler: who has won heaven, and who hell? O Qazi, which Kateb is it that you expound? All such readers and ponderers as you have come to ruin; none has gained (true) understanding. It is for love of woman that circumcision is done; I will not accept (it), brother. If God had meant to make me a Turk, O brother, (my circumcision) would have come about of itself. If one becomes a Turk by being circumcised, what is to be done about a woman? The wife, who shares half a man's body, does not leave his side; so one had best remain a Hindu. Leave (your arguments over) the Kateb and remember Ram, you crazed one: you are doing grievous wrong. Kabir has taken hold of Ram's support; the Turks have worn themselves out (in argument) and lost. ॥4॥
477.4: Raag Asa, the hymn of Bhagat Kabir Ji. As long as there is oil in the lamp and a wick in its mouth, everything can be seen; when the oil has burnt away the wick goes out, and the house becomes empty. O crazed one, (then) no one will keep you (in the house) even for a moment; repeat the Name of that Ram (who stands by you). Tell me, whose mother is she, whose father is he, which man's wife is she? When the pot (of the body) breaks, no one asks after (you); there is only: take him out, take him out. Sitting at the threshold the mother weeps; the brothers have taken up the bier and gone; her hair let loose, the wife weeps; (but) the swan (the soul) goes alone. Says Kabir: listen, O Sants, about the terrifying world-ocean: cruel suffering falls on this man's head, and Jam does not turn away, O Lord of the world.
478.1: Ik Oankar: God is One, the all-pervading Creator, realised through the True Guru's grace. Raag Asa, Chaupade Iktuke of Sri Kabir Ji. Sanak and Sanand did not find (God's) end; reading and reading the Vedas, Brahma wasted his life. Churn the churning of the Lord, O my brother; churn in Sahaj, so that the essence (the butter) is not lost. Make the body the churning pot, and the mind within it the churning staff; into this pot put the Shabad (as the culture that sets the milk). The churning of the Lord is the mind's reflection (on him); by the Guru's grace one obtains the stream of Amrit. Says Kabir: if the King (God) casts his glance of grace, then, holding to Ram's Name, one reaches the far shore. ॥4॥
478.2: Raag Asa, the hymn of Bhagat Kabir Ji. The wick has dried up, the oil is spent; the drum does not sound, the actor has lain down to sleep. The fire has gone out, no smoke rises; the One alone pervades all, there is no other. The string has snapped, the rebab does not play, (the rebab through which) one went astray and spoiled one's own work. The telling, the speaking, the saying and the getting said: when understanding dawned, the singing (of these) was forgotten. Says Kabir: those who crush the five (passions), from them the supreme state is not far. ॥4॥

In the Darpan's reading this tells of the state in which Maya's hold (the oil and the wick), its din (the drum) and craving (the fire) come to an end, and the actor (the mind), once made to dance by Maya, comes to rest.
478.3: Raag Asa, the hymn of Bhagat Kabir Ji. However many wrongs a son commits, his mother keeps none of them in her mind. O dear Ram, I am your child; why do you not destroy my faults? Even if (the child), in great anger, rushes at her again and again, even then the mother does not keep it in mind. My mind is caught in the whirl of worry; without (your) Name, how will it cross over? Give (this) body a pure understanding for ever, that Kabir may dwell on (your) virtues, steadily, in Sahaj. ॥4॥
478.4: Raag Asa, the hymn of Bhagat Kabir Ji. My Hajj, my bank of the Gomti, (is the place) where the Lord, the Pir in yellow robes, dwells. How beautiful the praise, Waah Waah, that (my mind) sings! The Lord's Name is dear to my mind. Narad and Sarad serve (him); beside (him) sits the Lady Kavla (Lakshmi) as his maidservant. My rosary at the neck is Ram on my tongue; uttering (his) thousand names over and over, I offer (him) my salaam. Says Kabir: I sing Ram's praises, and teach (this) to both Hindu and Turk. ॥4॥

Hajj: the Muslim pilgrimage to Mecca; the Gomti is a river held holy by Hindus, a tirath. Pitambar (clad in yellow) is a name of Vishnu; here, with Pir, it names God himself, whose dwelling, by the Darpan, is the mind.
Sarad (Sharda): Saraswati, the goddess of learning.
479.1: Raag Asa, nine Panchpade of Sri Kabir Ji, five of them Dutuke. Ik Oankar: God is One, the all-pervading Creator, realised through the True Guru's grace. The gardener woman plucks leaves, (but) in every leaf there is life; the stone for which she plucks the leaves, that stone is lifeless. Thus the gardener woman has gone astray: the True Guru is the deity who is awake. The leaves are Brahma, the branch Vishnu, the flowers Shankar (Shiva); you break off the three gods before your eyes: whose service, then, do you do? Carving the stone, (the sculptor) made the idol, setting his foot on its chest; if this idol is true, let it devour the one who carved it. Rice, lentils, lapsi and crisp kasar: the eater (the priest) has eaten them; this idol gets ashes in its mouth. The gardener woman has gone astray, the world has gone astray, (but) I have not gone astray; says Kabir: Ram, the Lord King, has kept me (from it) in his mercy. ॥5॥
Lapsi: a thin sweet pudding of flour, ghee and sugar; kasar: flour roasted in ghee with sugar. Food offered before an idol is afterwards eaten by its priests.
479.2: Raag Asa, the hymn of Bhagat Kabir Ji. Twelve years passed in childhood; for twenty years (more) he did no austerity at all; for thirty years he did no worship of God at all; then, grown old, he repented. Crying mine, mine, (his) life has gone; the ocean (of the body) has dried up, and the arms have lost their strength. He builds a bank in a dried-up pool, and with his own hands fences a field already reaped; the thief (death) came and at once carried off what the fool goes about guarding as his own. Feet, head and hands have begun to tremble; water flows from the eyes unchecked; no clear word comes from the tongue: and then, O brother, he hopes to practise dharma! (On whom) the Lord shows mercy, him he attunes (to himself), and he earns the profit of the Name of the Lord, Har Har; by the Guru's grace he found the Lord's wealth, which went with him when at the last he departed. Says Kabir: listen, O Sants: no one has taken any other wealth along; when the summons of Gopal, the King, came, (each) left wealth and mansions and went. ॥5॥
479.3: Raag Asa, the hymn of Bhagat Kabir Ji. To some (the Lord) has given silks and silken robes, to some beds woven with cotton tape; some have not even a rotten patched quilt, and in some homes (there is only) straw. Do not envy and quarrel, O mind; keep doing good deeds, and so earn (what you would have), O mind. The potter kneaded one and the same clay, and gave (the pots) colours of many kinds; in some he has set pearls and strings of pearls, and to some he has fastened sickness. To the miser wealth is given to keep; the fool says the wealth is his; when the rod of Jam strikes the head, in a moment (Jam) settles (the account). The Lord's servant is called the highest devotee; obeying (his) command he finds peace; whatever pleases him (the Lord), he accepts as true, and he enshrines (his) will in his mind. Says Kabir: listen, O Sants: (the cry of) mine, mine, is false; (death) tears open the cage and carries off the sparrow, and its little water pot and feeding cup are left behind. ॥5॥
480.1: Raag Asa, the hymn of Bhagat Kabir Ji. We are humble servants of God; you (O Qazi) love power in your mind. Allah, the First, the Master of the faith, does not command force (on anyone). O Qazi, what you say does not become (you). One keeps the roza, offers the namaz and recites the kalma, (yet by these) paradise is not won; seventy Kaabas are within the heart itself, if only one knows it. That is namaz, when one weighs (what is) justice; (that is) the kalma, when one knows (God) through understanding; (when) he subdues the five (passions), he spreads the prayer mat, and then he recognises the faith. Know the Master, keep compassion in your heart, and kill your pride, holding it worthless; when one comes to know himself and (so) knows others, then he gains a share in paradise. The clay is one, taking on many guises; in them (the one who knows) has recognised Brahm (God). Says Kabir: (O Qazi,) leaving paradise, your mind has taken to hell. ॥5॥
Qazi: the Muslim judge, who also taught the law of Islam. Roza, namaz and kalma: the fast, the daily prayer and the creed; the musalla is the prayer mat.

Satar: seventy, as elsewhere in Kabir's verse (ਸਤਰਿ ਸੈਇ, ਸਤਰਿ ਦੋਇ); seventy Kaabas, that is, many (the Shabdarth), the greatest Kaaba (the Santhya). The Darpan reads it as the Arabic sitr (a veil): the hidden Kaaba.
480.2: Raag Asa, the hymn of Bhagat Kabir Ji. In the city of the Gagan not one drop rains (now); where has the sound (nad) that was there merged? Has the supreme swan (the soul) departed, taking with it the Supreme Lord, the Supreme God, Madho (who dwelt within)? O Baba, where have they gone, who used to speak and who lived with the body, who danced in awareness, and told tales and talked? Where has the player gone, who made this mandar (the body, his drum)? No saying, no word, no awareness arises (now); (death) has drawn out all the vital light. Your companions, the ears, have grown feeble; the strength of the senses is spent; the feet have stopped, the hands have fallen limp, no word comes from the mouth. Worn out are the five enemies, all the thieves who roamed each after its own (pleasures); worn out is the elephant of the mind, worn out the heart, that moved about holding the thread of (the soul's) light. (All of them) have died, the ten fastenings have come loose, friends and brothers are all left behind; says Kabir: whoever meditates on the Lord breaks his bonds while still alive. ॥5॥

The yogis speak of nectar that drips from the Gagan and of the sound (nad) heard within in deep meditation. The ten fastenings: by the Santhya, the ten vital airs (pranas) that hold the body together.
By Bhai Vir Singh's Santhya and the Faridkot Teeka the shabad tells of a body the soul has left; the Darpan reads it as the mind that has died to the body's attachments.
480.3: Raag Asa, four Iktuke of Bhagat Kabir Ji. No one has more strength than the she-serpent (Maya), who beguiled (even) Brahma, Vishnu and Mahadev (Shiva). Striking and killing, the she-serpent has entered even the pure water; she who has stung the three worlds, by the Guru's grace I have seen (for what she is). Why do you keep crying she-serpent, she-serpent, O brother? Whoever has recognised the True One has devoured the she-serpent. Nothing else is as hollow as the she-serpent; when the she-serpent is conquered, what can poor Jam do? This she-serpent is of his (the Lord's) making; what strength or weakness can come from her (of herself)? While she dwells (in the mind), (the soul) dwells in bodies (again and again); by the Guru's grace Kabir has crossed over in Sahaj. ॥5॥
481.1: Raag Asa, the hymn of Bhagat Kabir Ji. What (use) is it to recite the Simritis to a dog? What (use) is it to sing the Lord's praises before a Saakat? Let us dwell on Ram, Ram, Ram, and stay absorbed (in him); (but) never, even by mistake, should we speak (of him) to a Saakat. What (use) is it to feed camphor to a crow? What (use) is it to give a snake milk to drink? Meeting the Sat Sangat, discerning understanding arises; touching the philosopher's stone, that same iron becomes gold. The Saakat, like the dog, does all that he is made to do; he does the deeds that were written (for him) from the beginning. Though one takes Amrit again and again to water the neem, says Kabir: its nature does not go. ॥5॥
481.2: Raag Asa, the hymn of Bhagat Kabir Ji. A fort like Lanka, a moat like the ocean: of that Ravan's house no trace is found. What shall I ask for? Nothing stays fixed; before my eyes the world is passing away. A hundred thousand sons and a hundred and twenty-five thousand grandsons: in that Ravan's house there is no lamp, no wick. He whose kitchen the moon and the sun kept heated, whose clothes the fire washed, (he too did not last). One who through the Guru's teaching makes (his mind) dwell in Ram's Name stays steadfast, and does not go anywhere. Says Kabir: listen, O people: without Ram's Name there is no liberation. ॥5॥
Ravan, the demon king of Lanka in the Ramayana, whose fort the ocean ringed like a moat; by tradition he held the gods in his service.
Loi: by the Darpan, people, the world (ਰੇ is the masculine address; the feminine is ਰੀ); by tradition, Loi was also the name of Kabir's wife.
481.3: Raag Asa, the hymn of Bhagat Kabir Ji. First (came) the son, after him the mother; the guru has fallen at the feet of the disciple. Listen to one wonder, O brothers: before (our) eyes a lion is herding cows. The fish of the water has given birth in a tree; before (our) eyes the cat has carried off the dog. The branches, O brother, are below, the root above; on its trunk fruits and flowers have grown. Riding a horse, the buffalo goes to graze (it); the bullock is outside, (while) its load has come home. Says Kabir: whoever understands this verse, dwelling on Ram, comes to see everything clearly. Twenty-two Chaupade and Panchpade.

This shabad speaks in paradoxes; the commentators read them as the soul, pure as it came from God, fallen under the sway of the mind and the senses: by the Darpan the soul was first pure (puut) and afterwards came under Maya (maai); the guru is the soul and the disciple the mind, the lion the soul and the cows the senses.
The closing line counts Bhagat Kabir Ji's shabads in Raag Asa so far: thirteen Chaupade and nine Panchpade, twenty-two in all.
481.4: Raag Asa, eight Tipade of Sri Kabir Ji, seven of them Dutuke and one an Iktuka. Ik Oankar: God is One, the all-pervading Creator, realised through the True Guru's grace. He who made the body from a drop and kept it (safe) in the pit of fire (of the womb), kept (you) ten months in the mother's belly; then (once you were born) Maya clung (to you). O mortal, why have you clung to greed and lost the jewel of (human) birth? In the field of deeds (this body), won by (the deeds of) a past birth, you have not sown the seed (of the Name). From a child you have grown old; what was to happen has happened; when Jam comes and seizes you by the hair, why weep then? You hope to live (on), while Jam watches your breaths; the world is a juggler's show: O Kabir, remember (the Lord), and cast that die. ॥3॥
482.1: Raag Asa, the hymn of Bhagat Kabir Ji. Making my body the dyer's vat, I shall dye my mind with virtues; the five elements (in their good qualities) are my wedding guests; I shall take the wedding rounds with Ram, the King; my soul is dyed in his love. Sing, sing, O brides, the songs of joy: Ram, the King, my Husband, has come to my house. In the lotus of the navel I have set up the wedding altar, and the knowledge of God is recited (as the wedding hymn); I have found such a groom as Ram, the King: so great is my good fortune. Godly men and sages have come to see the wonder, the three hundred and thirty million (gods) in their sky-chariots; says Kabir: the one Husband, God, has married me and is taking me away. ॥3॥

In this shabad Kabir speaks as a bride wedded to God. The bhavar (laavan) are the rounds that bride and groom walk at the wedding; the vedi is the square set up for them to sit in. The three hundred and thirty million are, by tradition, the gods.
482.2: Raag Asa, the hymn of Bhagat Kabir Ji. I am tormented by my mother-in-law, dear to my father-in-law, and I fear the very name of my husband's elder brother, O brother; O friends and companions, my husband's sister holds me fast, and I burn, parted from my husband's younger brother. My mind has gone mad, I have forgotten Ram: how shall I live my life, O brother? (My Husband Lord) dwells on my bed, (yet) I do not see him with my eyes: to whom shall I tell this pain, O brother? My stepfather quarrels (with me), and I am ever drunk with Maya; when I was with my elder brother, then I was dear to my Husband. Says Kabir: (all are caught in) the quarrel with the five (passions); quarrelling, (people) have wasted their lives; the whole world is bound by false Maya; (but) dwelling on Ram, I have found peace. ॥3॥

The soul speaks as a bride in her in-laws' house. By the Darpan the mother-in-law is Maya, the father-in-law the love of the body, the husband's elder brother death, his sister the senses and his younger brother discernment; the stepfather is the body, and the elder brother, with whom she was in the womb, the knowledge of God.
482.3: Raag Asa, the hymn of Bhagat Kabir Ji. In my house is thread, which I stretch into the warp every day; round your neck is the sacred thread. You, for your part, read the Vedas and the Gayatri; Gobind is in my heart. On my tongue is Bisan (Vishnu), in my eyes Narayan, and in my heart dwells Gobind. When Mukand (the giver of liberation) questions you at Jam's door, what answer will you give then, you crazed one? We are the cows and you our masters, the herdsmen, our keepers birth after birth; (yet) you have never taken us across the river to graze: what kind of masters are you? You are a Brahmin and I a weaver of Kashi; grasp what I have understood: you go begging from kings, the lords of the earth, while my mind is fixed on the Lord. ॥3॥
In this shabad Kabir speaks to a Brahmin; in the lines of the cows and the herdsmen, the herdsmen are the Brahmins, who call themselves the keepers of others.
482.4: Raag Asa, the hymn of Bhagat Kabir Ji. Life in the world is like a dream; life is the same as a dream. (Yet) taking it for true, we have tied it in our knot, letting go the supreme treasure. O Baba, (we) have given our love and attachment to Maya, which has robbed (us) of the jewel of wisdom. Seeing (the flame) with its eyes, the moth is caught; the foolish creature does not see the fire. (So) the fool, clinging to gold and woman, gives no thought to the noose of death. Reflect, and cast off your vices: he is the ship that carries (beings) across. Says Kabir: such is the Life of the world that there is no second (like him). ॥3॥
ਜਗਿ ਜੀਵਨੁ in the first line (two words) is life in the world; ਜਗਜੀਵਨੁ in the last line (one word) is the Life of the world, God.
482.5: Raag Asa, the hymn of Bhagat Kabir Ji. Many were the forms (births) I took, but now there will be no form again. The thread, the string and all the gear are worn out; (my mind) has come under the sway of Ram's Name. Now dancing comes no more to me; my mind does not beat the drum. Lust, anger and Maya I have burnt away; the pitcher of craving has burst. The robe of lust has grown old; doubt is gone, and all of it is left behind. I have known all beings as one; disputes and quarrels are over. Says Kabir: I have found the Perfect One; Ram has shown his grace. ॥3॥
The image is a dancer's: in birth after birth the soul took many guises and danced (at Maya's bidding) with its thread, string and drum (the Darpan: the thread and the string of attachment).
483.1: Raag Asa, the hymn of Bhagat Kabir Ji. (The Qazi) keeps the roza, seeks to please Allah, and for his palate's sake kills living beings; he looks to himself and not to others: why does he toil in vain? O Qazi, your one Master is within you, yet you do not ponder and look. You take no heed, you who are crazed by your creed; and so your life counts for nothing. The Kateb say that Allah is true, and is neither woman nor man. Reading and pondering are of no avail, O crazed one, if there is no awareness in the heart. Allah is hidden within every body; reflect on this in your heart. In both, Hindu and Muslim, is the One alone: Kabir proclaims it aloud. ॥3॥
483.2: Raag Asa, a Tipada Iktuka of Bhagat Kabir Ji. I adorned myself to meet (my Husband), but Hari, the Life of the world, the Lord of the world, has not met me. Hari is my Husband, I am Hari's young bride; Ram is great, and I a tiny little girl. Bride and Husband dwell together in one place; the bed is one, but meeting is hard. Blessed is the wedded bride who is pleasing to her Beloved; says Kabir: she does not come into birth again. ॥3॥
483.3: Raag Asa, Dupade of Sri Kabir Ji. Ik Oankar: God is One, the all-pervading Creator, realised through the True Guru's grace. When the diamond (the soul) has pierced the Diamond (God), the mind, restless as the wind, stays merged in Sahaj; this Diamond has pierced every light (every being): through the True Guru's words I have come to know (it). Through the Lord's praise, the unstruck (Anahad) Bani, (the soul) becomes a swan and recognises the Diamond. Says Kabir: I have seen such a Diamond, pervading the world; the hidden Diamond became manifest when the Guru who has reached him showed (him) to me. ॥2॥
Dupade: hymns of two stanzas each. The swan (hans) is held to pick out pearls and to part milk from water; here it is the soul that has gained the discernment to know the Lord.
483.4: Raag Asa, the hymn of Bhagat Kabir Ji. The first (bride) was ugly, of ill breeding and of evil ways, bad in her husband's home and bad in her parents'. The present one is beautiful, wise and of good ways; in Sahaj I have kept her within me. It is well that my first wedded one has died; may the one I hold now live age after age. Says Kabir: when the younger came, the elder lost her married fortune; the younger now stays with me, and the elder has found another. ॥2॥
By the Darpan the two brides are two states of the mind (the Santhya: kumati and sumati, the evil and the good understanding): the first proud and turned to Maya, the second humble and turned to God.
484.1: Raag Asa, the hymn of Bhagat Kabir Ji. My young bride was named Dhania (the wealthy one); (the holy men) have taken her and named her Ramjania (Ram's handmaid). These shaven-headed (holy men) have laid my house waste; they have set (my) little son to repeating Ram's Name. Says Kabir: listen, O my mother: these shaven-headed ones have made me lose my caste. ॥2॥

By the Darpan the whole shabad is Kabir's own: the bride is his soul, once fond of wealth and now Ram's handmaid, the little son his mind, and the shaven-headed ones the holy men of his company. By an old tradition (Bhai Vir Singh's Santhya), the first four lines are his mother's complaint and the last two his answer.
484.2: Raag Asa, the hymn of Bhagat Kabir Ji. Stop, stop, O young bride, do not draw your veil; at the end you will not get even half (a damri). Those before you went (from here) with their veils drawn; take care that their way does not cling to you. This is all the honour the veil brings: for ten days or five, (people say) a fine bride has come. Your veil is true only then, if, singing the Lord's praises, you leap and dance. Says Kabir: the bride wins only then, when her life passes in singing the Lord's praises. ॥4॥
The bride is the soul; her veil, by the Darpan, is her hiding her face from the Husband Lord. The damri was the smallest coin.
484.3: Raag Asa, the hymn of Bhagat Kabir Ji. Better the saw than your turning your back (on me); hold me to your heart, hear my plea. I am a sacrifice to you: turn your face (to me), Beloved; why do you kill me by turning your back on me? Even if you cleave my body, I will not draw back a limb; even if my body falls, I will not break my love. Between you and me there is no gap; you are that Husband, and I that wife. Says Kabir: listen, O people: now I put no trust in you. ॥4॥
Karvat (the saw): by the Santhya, a saw at Kashi (and Prayag) under which people had their bodies cut, hoping for liberation.
484.4: Raag Asa, the hymn of Bhagat Kabir Ji. No one has known the secret of the Weaver, who has brought forth the whole world and stretched it as his warp. While you (pandits) were listening to the Vedas and the Puranas, in that time I stretched out this little warp. He has made the earth and the sky his loom-comb; the moon and the sun he has set going side by side, two shuttles. With the pair of treadles he has made one play; in that Weaver the weaver's mind is content. The weaver has recognised his own home, and known Ram within his heart. Says Kabir: when he breaks the loom-comb, the Weaver blends thread into thread. ॥4॥

The weaver's terms: the warp (tana) is the threads stretched lengthwise; the karghah, by the Darpan and the Faridkot Teeka, the comb of the loom; the saath, the shuttles; the paai jor, the pair of treadles the weaver works with his feet. The Weaver is God; Kabir himself was a weaver.
484.5: Raag Asa, the hymn of Bhagat Kabir Ji. If one with filth within bathes at places of pilgrimage, he shall not go to Baikunth (heaven). Nothing comes of satisfying people: Ram is not ignorant. Worship Ram alone, the one divine Lord; the true bath is service to the Guru. If liberation came by dipping in water, frogs bathe day after day; as are the frogs, so are those men: again and again they come into birth. One hard of heart who dies at Banaras cannot be spared hell; if the Lord's saint dies in Haramb (the barren land of Magahar), he carries all the people across. Where there is no day and no night, no Veda and no Shastra, there dwells the Formless Lord. Says Kabir: meditate on him, O men, O crazed world. ॥4॥
By an old belief, whoever dies at Banaras (Kashi) is liberated, and whoever dies at Magahar is born again as a donkey.
485.1: Ik Oankar: God is One, the all-pervading Creator, realised through the True Guru's grace. Raag Asa, the hymn of Sri Namdev Ji. The One, in many (forms), is pervading and filling all; wherever I look, there is he. (Beings are) bewitched by the many-coloured pictures of Maya; rare is the one who understands. All is Gobind, all is Gobind; without Gobind there is nothing. As on a single thread are strung beads by the hundred and the thousand, so God is woven through (all), warp and weft. The waves, the foam and the bubbles of water are not apart from the water; this world is the play of the Supreme Lord: on reflection, it is not other (than him). False doubt and dream-like desires (men) have taken for true things. The Guru taught (me) a mind set on good; on waking, my mind was convinced. Says Namdev: look at the Lord's creation, reflecting on it in your heart: within every heart, and evenly in all, is the one Murari alone. ॥4॥
485.2: Raag Asa, the hymn of Bhagat Namdev Ji. I brought a pitcher and had it filled with water, to bathe the Thakur (the image of the Lord); in the water live forty-two lakh beings; Bithal was (already) there: what should I do it for? Wherever I go, there is Bithal, ever at play in supreme bliss. I brought flowers and strung a garland, to worship the Thakur; the bumblebee has taken their fragrance first; Bithal was (already) there: what should I do it for? I brought milk and had kheer cooked, to offer as food to the Thakur; the calf has first made the milk his leavings; Bithal was (already) there: what should I do it for? Below is Bithal, above is Bithal; without Bithal there is no world. In every place and between places, prays Nama, you are filling all the earth. ॥4॥

Bithal (Vitthal): Namdev's name for God; in this shabad the image is called the Thakur, and the all-pervading Lord Bithal. By tradition, forty-two lakh of the eighty-four lakh species of beings live in water.
485.3: Raag Asa, the hymn of Bhagat Namdev Ji. My mind is the yardstick, my tongue the scissors; measuring and measuring, I cut Jam's noose. What would I do with caste? what with lineage? I repeat the Name of Ram day and night. I dye in the dyeing vat, I sew the seams; without Ram's Name I do not live a ghari. I worship in devotion, I sing the Lord's praises; at all hours I meditate on my Master. The needle is of gold, the thread of silver; Nama's mind is attached to the Lord. ॥4॥
Namdev speaks in the terms of his trade (printing and sewing cloth): the yardstick, the scissors, the dyeing vat, the needle and the thread. Paati: lineage, the clan within a caste.
485.4: Raag Asa, the hymn of Bhagat Namdev Ji. The snake sheds its slough, but does not shed its poison; as the heron stands in the water, fixed in meditation. Why practise meditation and chanting, while one's own mind is not pure? The man who knows the lion's way of food (a living got by violence), such a one is called the god of cheats. Nama's Master has put an end to (his) strife: drink the elixir of Ram, O stone-hearted one. ॥3॥
Singhach bhojan: the lion's food, a living got by force and deceit. Dagra: by the Darpan a Marathi word for stone, the stone-hearted; the Santhya also reads it as the path, or as deceiver.
486.1: Raag Asa, the hymn of Bhagat Namdev Ji. Those who come to know the Supreme Lord have no liking for (other) hopes; Ram keeps free of care the minds of the devotees who have kept him in mind. O mind, how will you swim across? The world-ocean is full of the water of the pleasures of the senses. Seeing false Maya, O mind, you have gone astray. (God) gave (me) birth in a calico printer's home, (yet) the Guru's teaching came to (me); by the grace of the Sants, Nama has met the Lord. ॥2॥
486.2: Raag Asa, the hymn of Sri Ravidas Ji. Ik Oankar: God is One, the all-pervading Creator, realised through the True Guru's grace. The deer, the fish, the bumblebee, the moth and the elephant are each destroyed by a single failing; how much hope (of escape) is there, then, for one in whom are five failings that cannot be subdued? O Madho, (man) has given his love to ignorance; (so) the lamp of (his) discernment is clouded. The creatures of the species that move crookedly are without thought; for them to give no thought to good deeds and sins is natural; (but) human birth is hard to come by, and still its company is with the low (vices). Wherever beings and creatures go (to be born), in the power of their deeds, death's noose, which cannot be cut, is upon them; no remedy avails. O servant Ravidas, turn away (from vice) and give up doubt; the Guru's wisdom is the austerity of austerities. O remover of your devotees' fears, grant (me) supreme bliss at the last. ॥4॥

Each creature dies through one sense: the deer through hearing (the hunter's bell), the fish through taste (the bait), the bumblebee through smell (shut in the lotus), the moth through sight (the flame), and the elephant through touch (lured by lust into a pit). Man has all five.
486.3: Raag Asa, the hymn of Bhagat Ravidas Ji. (O God,) the Sants are your own form, and their fellowship is your life; through the True Guru's wisdom one comes to know the Sants (as such), O God of gods. The company of the Sants, the relish of the Sants' discourse (of God), and love for the Sants: give (these) to me, O God of gods. (Give me too) the conduct of the Sants, the path of the Sants, and service to the servants of the Sants. One thing more I ask: devotion, the wish-fulfilling jewel (Chintamani); do not let me set eyes on the unholy and the sinners. Says Ravidas: the one who knows (this) is the one who truly knows: the Sants and the Infinite One are not apart. ॥4॥
Several words of this shabad are Marathi: chi, cho, cha (of), majhai (to me), olhag (a servant), olhagani (service).
486.4: Raag Asa, the hymn of Bhagat Ravidas Ji. You are sandalwood, we are the lowly castor plant, (yet we have) a dwelling beside you; from a lowly tree we have been raised high; (your) scent, a sweet scent, has come to dwell (in us). O Madho, (I have taken) the refuge of your Sat Sangat; we are full of faults, you are the doer of good. You are silk, white and yellow; we are like wretched worms; O Madho, may we stay joined to the Sat Sangat, as honeybees to the comb. Low in caste, low in lineage, low is my birth; and I have not served Ram, the Sovereign Lord, says Ravidas the Chamar (of the leather-working caste). ॥3॥
486.5: Raag Asa, the hymn of Bhagat Ravidas Ji. What does it matter if (my) body falls to pieces? Only if love should go does your servant fear. (O God,) your lotus feet are the dwelling of (my) mind; drinking (their nectar), I have found, yes found, the wealth of beloved Ram. Prosperity, adversity and wealth are the veils of Maya; your servant is not lost in them. Your servant is bound with the rope of (your) love; says Ravidas: what good would there be in getting free (of it)? ॥3॥
487.1: Raag Asa, the hymn of Bhagat Ravidas Ji. Har, Har, Har, Har, Har, Har, Har: remembering the Lord, (his) servants have crossed over, wholly saved. Through the Lord's Name Kabir became renowned, and the papers (of the accounts) of birth after birth were torn up. By virtue of it Namdev gave (the Lord) milk to drink, and so he did not come into the pains of birth in the world. The servant Ravidas is dyed in the love of Ram; so, through the Guru's grace, he does not go to hell. See how this puppet of clay dances! It looks and looks about, listens, speaks, and runs here and there. When it gains something, it grows proud; when Maya is gone, it begins to weep. In mind, word and deed it is lured by tastes, sweet and sharp; when it perishes, (the soul) goes and is absorbed somewhere (else). Says Ravidas: the world is (a juggler's) show, O brother; my love has been formed with the Juggler (who stages it). ॥3॥
This verse holds two shabads; the second begins at Mati ko putra, with its own Rahao.
By tradition the boy Namdev set milk before the Lord and would not rise until the Lord drank it.
487.2: Raag Asa, the hymn of Bhagat Dhanna Ji. Ik Oankar: God is One, the all-pervading Creator, realised through the True Guru's grace. Wandering and roaming, many births have gone by; body, mind and wealth never hold steady. Steeped in greed, poison and lust, the greedy one has let God, the diamond, slip from his mind. The poison fruits tasted sweet (to you), O crazed mind, and you knew nothing of noble reflection; love of other kinds grew, away from virtue, and the warp of birth and death was stretched again. Knowing the way (to live), you did not settle it in your heart; burning (in craving), you have fallen into Jam's net and noose. O mind, you gathered and stored poison fruits so (much) that God, the Supreme Being, slipped from the mind. (Those to whom) the Guru gave the wealth of entry into knowledge, their attention, faith and mind became one (with God); they embraced loving devotion, came to know peace, and, filled and fully content, were set free. The one in whom (God's) all-pervading Light has merged has recognised God, who cannot be deceived. Dhanna has gained the wealth, the Upholder of the earth (Dharnidhar); meeting the humble Sants, he has merged (in him). ॥4॥
487.3: By the Fifth Guru (Guru Arjan Dev Ji). Namdev's mind was absorbed in Gobind, Gobind, Gobind; the poor calico printer, worth half a dam (a copper coin), came to be worth lakhs. Leaving his weaving and warping, Kabir turned his love to (the Lord's) feet; the humble weaver of a low family became an ocean of virtue. Ravidas used to carry (dead) cattle every day; he gave up Maya, grew renowned in the Saadh Sangat, and was granted the sight of the Lord. Sain the barber, who ran errands (for people), came to be known in every house; the Supreme Lord came to live in his heart, and he was numbered among the devotees. Hearing of this, the humble Jatt (Dhanna) rose and set himself to devotion; the Lord of the world met him face to face; most fortunate was Dhanna. ॥4॥
This shabad is the Fifth Guru's, set among Bhagat Dhanna Ji's; it tells what moved Dhanna to devotion.
488.1: O my mind, why do you not remember the merciful Damodar? Know no other (as your support). Though you run through the lands of the universe, that alone comes about which the Creator does. In the mother's womb, in its water, he made the body with its ten doors; giving it food, he keeps it (safe) in the fire (of the womb): such is our Master. The she-turtle lives in the water, her young outside it; they have no wings, and (she has) no milk (for them); (yet) the Perfect One, Supreme Bliss, the Enchanter of hearts, (cares for them): understand and see this in your mind. A worm lies hidden inside a stone, with no way out for it; says Dhanna: it too is in the care of the Perfect One; have no fear, O soul. ॥3॥
488.2: Raag Asa, the hymn of Sheikh Farid Ji. Ik Oankar: God is One, the all-pervading Creator, realised through the True Guru's grace. Those whose love (for God) is from the heart are the true (lovers); those with one thing in their mind and another on their lips are called raw (in love). (Those) steeped in the love of God (Khuda) are dyed in the colour of his sight; those who have forgotten the Name have become a burden on the earth. Those whom (God) has himself attached to his hem are the dervishes at (his) door; blessed is the mother who bore them; their coming (into the world) bears fruit. O Sustainer, you are boundless, beyond reach, without end. Those who have known the True One: I kiss their feet. Your shelter (is mine), O God; you are the Forgiver; grant Sheikh Farid the alms of (your) worship (bandagi). ॥4॥
488.3: Raag Asa, the hymn of Sheikh Farid Ji. Says Sheikh Farid: O dear one, hold fast to Allah; this body will become dust in its humble home, the grave. Union (with God) can be today, O Sheikh Farid, if the little cranes (the senses) that inflame the mind are held back. If I know that we must die and not come round again, (then) we should not waste ourselves clinging to the false world. Let us speak the truth, speak what is right, and speak no falsehood; the way the Guru shows, let us walk it as his disciples. The handsome young men cross to the far bank, and (seeing it) the fair maiden's heart takes courage; (but) those who turned to the side of gold were cut through with the saw. O Sheikh, in this world no one's life has lasted for ever; on the seat where we now sit, many have sat and gone. Cranes in Katik, forest fires in Chet, lightning in Savan, and in winter (a wife's) arms about her husband's neck look lovely. (So) those who must go are going; reflect on this in your mind. Six months it takes to shape (the body), a single instant to break it. The earth asks the sky, O Farid: where have the boatmen gone? (The answer:) they are passing their time in the graves, and the souls are bearing the reproaches. ॥8॥

Cranes come to the plains in Katik (October to November) and fly off when the season ends; in the Rahao they are the restless senses. Forests catch fire in Chet (March to April), and lightning flashes in Savan (July to August): each comes in its season and is gone.
The boatmen: by the Darpan, the great leaders of the world; by Bhai Vir Singh's Santhya, the souls that steer the boat of the body.

347.1: There is one God, Ik Oankar, the One who pervades all and is ever the same; his Name is Sat (the One who truly is); he is the Creator, the Being who dwells in all, without fear, without enmity, his form beyond time, unborn, self-existent, realised by the Guru's grace.
Raag Asa, Ghar 1, by the First Guru (Guru Nanak Dev Ji): So Dar.
What is that gate of yours like, and what is that home like, where (you) sit and take care of all?
The sounds of your countless instruments of many kinds play there, and so many are the musicians who play for you.
So many of your ragas, with their raginis, are sung there, and so many are your singers.
Wind, water and fire sing of you; Dharam Raj (the judge of souls) sings of you at your door.
Chitr and Gupt, who know how to write, sing of you; what they write, Dharam Raj weighs and judges.
Shiva, Brahma and the goddesses sing of you, ever beautiful, adorned by you.
The Indras, seated on their thrones, sing of you with the gods at your door.
The Siddhas sing of you in samadhi (deep meditative absorption); the sadhus sing of you in contemplation.
The celibates, the charitable and the contented sing of you; the mighty heroes sing of you.
The learned pandits and the great rishis sing of you, age after age, along with the Vedas.
The enchanting women who charm the mind sing of you, in heaven, in the mortal world and in the netherworld.
All the jewels you have created sing of you, along with the sixty-eight places of pilgrimage.
Warriors of great might and heroes sing of you; the four sources of life sing of you.
The regions, the worlds and the universes, made and set in place by you, sing of you.
They alone sing of you who please you, your devotees, steeped (in your love) and full of delight.
So many others sing of you who do not come to my mind; what can Nanak consider?
He, he alone, is ever true; the Master is true, and true is his glory.
He is, and he will be; he does not depart, nor will he depart, he who made the creation.
He who brought forth Maya of many colours, many kinds and many species
watches over what he has made, having made it, as befits his greatness.
Whatever pleases him, that he will do; no command can then be given (to him).
He is the King, the Emperor over kings; O Nanak, (our part is) to live in his will. ॥1॥
348.1: Raag Asa, by the Fourth Guru (Guru Ram Das Ji).

That Purakh, the Being who pervades all, is Niranjan, free of the stain of Maya (the world's illusion and lure); the Lord, the all-pervading Being, is free of that stain; the Lord is beyond reach, wholly beyond reach, without limit.
O Lord, the eternal Creator, all meditate on you, all meditate on you.
All beings are yours, Lord; you are the Giver to every being.
Meditate on the Lord, revered Sants (saints): he makes all sorrows pass away.
The Lord himself is the Master, and the Lord himself the servant; O Nanak, what is a poor creature (by itself)?
You are within every heart, and in all without any gap; O Lord, you, the one Being, pervade all.
Some are givers and some are beggars; all these are your wondrous plays.
You are the giver yourself, and yourself the one who enjoys (the gifts); apart from you I know no other.
You are the Supreme Lord (Paarbrahm), endless, endless; which of your virtues shall I name and describe?
Those who serve you, those who serve you, Lord: your servant Nanak is a sacrifice to them.
O Lord, those who meditate on you, who meditate on you, live at peace in the world.
Liberated, liberated are those who have meditated on the Lord; the noose of Jam has snapped for them.
Those who have meditated on the Fearless, on the Fearless Lord: he takes away all their fear.
Those who have served, who have served my Lord, merge into the very form of the Lord, Har Har.
Blessed, blessed are those who have meditated on the Lord; your servant Nanak gives himself in sacrifice to them.
The storehouses of devotion to you, of devotion to you, Lord, are full beyond end, beyond all end.
Your devotees, your devotees praise you, O Lord, many, countless, without end.
Many, so many, worship you, O Lord; numberless (beings) practise austerities and repeat (your Name).
Many, so many of yours read the many Simritis and Shastras, and carry out the rites and the six duties.
O servant Nanak, those devotees, those devotees alone are good who please my Lord God.
You are the Primal Being, beyond the farthest beyond, the Creator, Lord; no other is as great as you.
In every age you are the One; always, always you are the One; you are the unmoving Creator, ever the same.
O Lord, whatever pleases you yourself, that alone comes about; whatever you yourself do, that takes place.
You yourself brought forth the whole creation, and you yourself, having made it, have destroyed it all.
Servant Nanak sings the virtues of the Creator, who knows each and every one. ॥5॥
348.2: Ik Oankar: God is One, the all-pervading Creator, realised through the True Guru's grace.
Raag Asa, Ghar 2, Chaupade, by the First Guru (Guru Nanak Dev Ji).
Everyone calls you great, (O God,) having heard (it from others),
but how great you are is (told) only on seeing you.
Your worth cannot be fixed, nor can you be put into words.
Those who speak of you stay merged in you.
O my great Master, deep and profound, fathomless in virtues,
no one knows how much, how vast, your expanse is.
All who practise surat (attention fixed on God) joined together and practised it;
all who weigh worth joined together and weighed (yours);
yet by the men of knowledge, the men of meditation, the teachers and the teachers of teachers,
not even a sesame seed's worth of your greatness could be told.
All truthfulness, all austerities, all good deeds,
and the great powers of the Siddhas, the accomplished ones:
without you, no one has attained this siddhi (accomplishment).
It comes by (your) grace, and then no one can hold it back.
What can the poor speaker (say)?
Your storehouses are filled with praises.
The one to whom you give (your praise), what can anyone do against him?
O Nanak, the True One (himself) is the one who adorns (him). ॥4॥
349.1: Raag Asa, by the First Guru (Guru Nanak Dev Ji).
When I utter (his Name), I live; when it is forgotten, I die.
The True Name is hard to utter.
If hunger for the True Name arises,
then, eating (of the Name) in that hunger, the sorrows are driven away.
Why should he be forgotten, O my mother?
The Master is true, and (is found) through the True Name.
Of the True Name's greatness, even a sesame seed's worth,
they have grown weary telling, yet none has found its worth.
If all were to join together and set about describing him,
he does not become greater, nor does he become less.
He does not die, nor is there mourning (for him).
He keeps on giving, and what he gives to be enjoyed never runs out.
This is his quality: there is no other (like him);
none has been, and none will be.
As great as you yourself are, so great is your gift,
(you,) who made the day and made the night.
Those who forget the Master are low-born;
O Nanak, those without the Name are the outcastes. ॥4॥
349.2: Raag Asa, by the First Guru (Guru Nanak Dev Ji).
If a beggar at the door cries out, the Master within the mansion hears (his cry);
whether he gives him comfort or pushes him away, it is honour he gives him all the same.
Recognise the light (of God in all), and do not ask anyone's caste; hereafter there is no caste.
(God) himself makes (beings) act, and himself acts,
and himself takes to heart (their) grievances.
(O God,) when you, the Creator, are the doer of all,
what dependence on anyone is there, and what is the world?
(God) himself creates (beings), and himself gives (to them);
he himself holds them back from evil-mindedness.
By the Guru's grace, (in whose) mind (God) comes to dwell,
from within (that one) pain and darkness depart.
(God) himself makes the Truth dear (to a being);
to others (he) does not give the Truth.
Says Nanak: if (he) gives (it) to anyone, he calls (that one) to no account hereafter. ॥4॥
349.3: Raag Asa, by the First Guru (Guru Nanak Dev Ji).
The workings of the mind are the cymbals and the ankle-bells;
the (love of the) world is the drum: these are the instruments that play.
The mind, a Narad, dances: this is the sway of Kalyug;
where can the celibate and the virtuous set their feet?
O Nanak, be a sacrifice to the Name.
The world is blind; the Master (alone) knows all.
The disciple, on the contrary, eats from the guru;
for love of bread he comes to live in (the guru's) house.
Even if (one were given) a hundred years of living and eating,
only that day is approved on which (one) recognises the Master.
No compassion stirs at the sight of (one in need);
no one does without give and take.
The king does justice (only) if (something) comes into (his) hand;
if one appeals in God's name, no one heeds.
Says Nanak: in form and in name one is human,
but in deeds a dog that obeys orders at (its master's) door (for scraps).
If by the Guru's grace (one) knows (oneself) a guest (here),
then (one) gains some honour in the Lord's court. ॥4॥
350.1: Raag Asa, by the First Guru (Guru Nanak Dev Ji).
(O God,) all the speaking and hearing there is, is your own current of life; all the form there is, is your body.
You yourself are the one who tastes, you yourself the life that dwells (in all); O mother, I can speak of no other, no second.
he is One, brother, he alone is One.
(He) himself kills and himself sets free; himself he takes and gives.
(He) himself watches over (all), himself delights, himself casts his glance of grace.
Whatever is to be done, (he) himself is doing; nothing else can be done.
As (he) acts, so is (he) named; (O God,) all this is your greatness.
Kalyug is the woman who sells wine, Maya the sweet wine, and the drunken mind keeps on drinking.
(God) himself makes forms of many kinds; this is what poor Nanak says. ॥4॥
350.2: Raag Asa, by the First Guru (Guru Nanak Dev Ji).
Let wisdom be the instrument, and love the drum (the pakhavaj);
(then) bliss arises, and the mind is ever full of zest.
This is devotion, this the practice of austerity;
Dance in this joy, setting your feet down with care.
One who knows (how to sing God's) praise keeps the full beat;
any other dancing is only the pleasures and the whims of the mind.
Let truth and contentment be the two cymbals that play;
let being ever in bloom be the bells upon the feet;
let having no love for another be the raag and its music;
Dance in this joy, setting your feet down with care.
Let the fear (of God), held in heart and mind, be the whirling turn,
whether sitting or rising, always and ever;
let knowing the body to be ashes be the rolling on the ground;
Dance in this joy, setting your feet down with care.
Let there be love for the teaching in the gathering of the Sikhs,
hearing the True Name through the Guru,
and, O Nanak, uttering it again and again;
Dance in this joy, setting your feet down with care. ॥4॥
350.3: Raag Asa, by the First Guru (Guru Nanak Dev Ji).
(O Lord, you) brought forth the air and set the whole earth in place, and bound water and fire together.
Blind (in his folly), the ten-headed (Ravan) had his own head cut off; did killing Ravan make (you) any greater?
What praise of you can be spoken?
You fill all, pervading every one.
Creating the beings, you hold the way (of their lives) in your hand; did putting a nose-rope on Kali (the serpent) make (you) any greater?
Whose husband are you, and whom is one to call your wife? You pervade all, with no gap between.
Brahma, the giver of boons, went with his family into the (lotus) stalk to search out (the source of) creation;
going on, he found no end to it. Did slaying Kans make (you) any greater?
(You) brought forth the jewels; the ocean of milk was churned, and the others (gods and demons) cried out in anger: We did this.
Says Nanak, how can the hidden (Lord) stay hidden? (It was he who) shared out (the jewels) one by one. ॥4॥
351.1: Raag Asa, by the First Guru (Guru Nanak Dev Ji).
Deeds and conduct grew into a spreading vine, and its fruit was the Name of the Lord (Ram).
It has no form or outline; the Shabad that the Pure Lord made sounds (within), unstruck.
If anyone comes to know (the Lord) and tells (of him),
Those who drank it became rapt with joy; their bonds and nooses broke.
Within (them), (their) light merged in the Light; then they gave up (chasing) the gains of Maya.
(O Lord, they) saw your form in every light, and your Maya in all the worlds.
In this (world), a form of strife, (the Lord) sits apart, unattached, and, present within (all) as his own reflection, keeps watch (over all).
(Such a) yogi plays the vina of the Shabad, (rapt) in the sight of the Infinite One's form;
through the unstruck Shabad he is dyed in the Husband Lord: this is the reflection Nanak speaks. ॥4॥
351.2: Raag Asa, by the First Guru (Guru Nanak Dev Ji).
(O Lord,) my virtues (are only these): loads of talk upon my head.
Of all talk, the (worthy) talk is (talk of) the Creator.
Eating, drinking, laughing are (all) in vain
as long as you do not come to mind in the heart.
Then what care is left (for anyone), and what (more) is there to do,
if, born into this (human) life, one takes what is worth the taking?
